slides.text:
Observed behavior : a release script runs "cat .git/refs/heads/main" and finds no file; a variant greps
                    packed-refs and stamps the build with last week's commit
Git state         : main was packed by git gc (or arrived packed from git clone), then moved on
Mechanism         : lookup reads the loose file first and packed-refs second; maintenance moves loose
                    refs into packed-refs; a later update writes a new loose file and leaves the old line
Root cause        : the scripts read one of several storage locations instead of asking Git
Why Git does this : one file per ref wastes space and is slow with thousands of refs
Correct fix       : git rev-parse --verify refs/heads/main
Prevention        : never read .git/refs or packed-refs from a script; use rev-parse, for-each-ref,
                    update-ref and symbolic-ref, which also work with reftable

lines.s: # One line per fetched branch: object ID, a marker for "git pull", and where it came from.
# Used as a revision, FETCH_HEAD means its first line:
# A merge of two branches at once, stopped before the commit is made:
Automatic merge went well; stopped before committing as requested
# MERGE_HEAD holds one line per branch being merged. ORIG_HEAD holds where main was:
# The refs outside refs/, as Git lists them. The two pseudorefs are not in the list:
# A root ref is an ordinary ref, so update-ref writes it. A pseudoref is refused:
fatal: update_ref failed for ref 'MERGE_HEAD': refusing to update pseudoref 'MERGE_HEAD'
git reflog exists ORIG_HEAD; echo "exit status: $?"
# A branch of a teammate, fetched by path without a destination ref. It lands in FETCH_HEAD only:
# No ref under refs/ and no reflog entry names that commit, so fsck reports it.
# (The dangling tree is the result of the two-branch merge that was aborted above.)
# A garbage collection without a grace period deletes it. The name stays behind and names nothing:
# Root refs are listed. The two pseudorefs, FETCH_HEAD and MERGE_HEAD, are not:
# Pseudorefs can be read like refs, but update-ref refuses to write them:
fatal: update_ref failed for ref 'MERGE_HEAD': refusing to update pseudoref 'MERGE_HEAD'
fatal: update_ref failed for ref 'FETCH_HEAD': refusing to update pseudoref 'FETCH_HEAD'
# No operation is in progress. Three leftovers remain: FETCH_HEAD, ORIG_HEAD, and AUTO_MERGE,
# the tree that "git stash pop" merged. None of them describes unfinished work.

beats.text: The release script stamps every build with a commit ID. It gets that ID by reading the file .git/refs/heads/main. It has done so for years. On the new build image that file doesn't exist, and the release stops.

beats.text: It isn't. The branch exists and Git resolves it. The ref is stored somewhere else, and the script should have asked Git. A ref is a name that holds an object ID, and a branch is one kind of ref. This video shows every place a ref can be stored in the default format, and why no script should read any of them. Keep that missing file in mind. It comes back.

beats.text: In one sentence: a ref is a name that holds an object ID or the name of another ref, and in the default files format a ref is a small file under refs/, a line in packed-refs, or both.
beats.tele: In one sentence: a ref is a name that holds an object ID or the name of another ref, and in the default `files` format a ref is a small file under `refs/`, a line in `packed-refs`, or both.

beats.text: The glossary's definition: "a name that points to an object name or another ref (the latter is called a symbolic ref)". Names either start with refs/ or sit in the root of the hierarchy.
beats.tele: The glossary's definition: "a name that points to an object name or another ref (the latter is called a symbolic ref)". Names either start with `refs/` or sit in the root of the hierarchy.

beats.text: Under refs/: refs/heads/<name> is a local branch, moved by commit, merge, reset, rebase and git branch -f. refs/tags/<name> is a tag, pointing at a commit or at a tag object, meant to stay put. refs/remotes/<remote>/<name> is a remote-tracking branch, the last known position of a branch in that remote, moved by fetch and push. refs/stash is the newest stash entry, work you set aside, and older entries live in its reflog. And tools own namespaces such as refs/bisect/, refs/notes/ and refs/replace/.
beats.tele: Under `refs/`: `refs/heads/<name>` is a local branch, moved by commit, merge, reset, rebase and `git branch -f`. `refs/tags/<name>` is a tag, pointing at a commit or at a tag object, meant to stay put. `refs/remotes/<remote>/<name>` is a remote-tracking branch, the last known position of a branch in that remote, moved by fetch and push. `refs/stash` is the newest stash entry, work you set aside, and older entries live in its reflog. And tools own namespaces such as `refs/bisect/`, `refs/notes/` and `refs/replace/`.

beats.text: How they're stored in the files format. A loose ref is a file holding the ID and a newline. A symbolic ref is a file holding ref: and a name. packed-refs is one sorted text file with many refs. Why three forms? One file per ref wastes space and is slow with thousands of refs.
beats.tele: How they're stored in the `files` format. A loose ref is a file holding the ID and a newline. A symbolic ref is a file holding `ref:` and a name. `packed-refs` is one sorted text file with many refs. Why three forms? One file per ref wastes space and is slow with thousands of refs.

beats.text: The lookup rule is the heart of this video. Lookup reads the loose file first and packed-refs second. And, quoting the manual of git pack-refs: "subsequent updates to branches always create new files under $GIT_DIR/refs". So after packing, a branch that moves gets a loose file again, and the old line in packed-refs stays, stale. The loose file wins.
beats.tele: The lookup rule is the heart of this video. Lookup reads the loose file first and `packed-refs` second. And, quoting the manual of `git pack-refs`: "subsequent updates to branches always create new files under `$GIT_DIR/refs`". So after packing, a branch that moves gets a loose file again, and the old line in `packed-refs` stays, stale. The loose file wins.

beats.text: The plumbing works the same in every format. git for-each-ref lists and formats. git show-ref lists and verifies. git update-ref writes or deletes one ref with an optional check of its old value. git symbolic-ref reads and writes symbolic refs. git pack-refs moves loose refs into packed-refs without changing a value.
beats.tele: The plumbing works the same in every format. `git for-each-ref` lists and formats. `git show-ref` lists and verifies. `git update-ref` writes or deletes one ref with an optional check of its old value. `git symbolic-ref` reads and writes symbolic refs. `git pack-refs` moves loose refs into `packed-refs` without changing a value.

beats.text: Second topic: root refs. In one sentence: a few refs live directly in the repository directory, with names in capital letters that end in _HEAD. Two of them, FETCH_HEAD and MERGE_HEAD, aren't refs at all in the strict sense and are called pseudorefs.
beats.tele: Second topic: root refs. In one sentence: a few refs live directly in the repository directory, with names in capital letters that end in `_HEAD`. Two of them, `FETCH_HEAD` and `MERGE_HEAD`, aren't refs at all in the strict sense and are called pseudorefs.

beats.text: The glossary says a pseudoref has "different semantics than normal refs", can be read by normal Git commands, and cannot be written by commands like git update-ref. It lists two. FETCH_HEAD "may refer to multiple object IDs", each annotated with its source. MERGE_HEAD "contains all commit IDs which are being merged".
beats.tele: The glossary says a pseudoref has "different semantics than normal refs", can be read by normal Git commands, and cannot be written by commands like `git update-ref`. It lists two. `FETCH_HEAD` "may refer to multiple object IDs", each annotated with its source. `MERGE_HEAD` "contains all commit IDs which are being merged".

beats.text: A version note you need when you read older material. Before Git 2.46 the glossary called every special file under .git a pseudoref. Since Git 2.46, "pseudoref" means FETCH_HEAD and MERGE_HEAD only. The others are root refs, stored by the ref backend like any other ref. Say "root ref" for ORIG_HEAD and its relatives, and notice that older tutorials, and the description of --include-root-refs in the git for-each-ref manual, still use the old wording.
beats.tele: A version note you need when you read older material. Before Git 2.46 the glossary called every special file under `.git` a pseudoref. Since Git 2.46, "pseudoref" means `FETCH_HEAD` and `MERGE_HEAD` only. The others are root refs, stored by the ref backend like any other ref. Say "root ref" for `ORIG_HEAD` and its relatives, and notice that older tutorials, and the description of `--include-root-refs` in the `git for-each-ref` manual, still use the old wording.

beats.text: HEAD is written by git init, git switch and git checkout, and is never gone. ORIG_HEAD is written by merge, rebase, reset and git am, and on Git 2.55 also by git stash push. It holds where HEAD was before, until the next such command overwrites it.
beats.tele: `HEAD` is written by `git init`, `git switch` and `git checkout`, and is never gone. `ORIG_HEAD` is written by merge, rebase, reset and `git am`, and on Git 2.55 also by `git stash push`. It holds where HEAD was before, until the next such command overwrites it.

beats.text: FETCH_HEAD is written by fetch and pull. MERGE_HEAD is written by a merge that stops, and goes when the merge is committed or aborted. CHERRY_PICK_HEAD and REVERT_HEAD are written by a cherry-pick or revert that stops or runs with --no-commit.
beats.tele: `FETCH_HEAD` is written by fetch and pull. `MERGE_HEAD` is written by a merge that stops, and goes when the merge is committed or aborted. `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` and `REVERT_HEAD` are written by a cherry-pick or revert that stops or runs with `--no-commit`.

beats.text: REBASE_HEAD is written by a rebase that stops. BISECT_HEAD is written by git bisect --no-checkout. AUTO_MERGE is written by the ort merge machinery when it leaves conflicts, and on Git 2.55 also by a clean git stash pop. It holds a tree.
beats.tele: `REBASE_HEAD` is written by a rebase that stops. `BISECT_HEAD` is written by `git bisect --no-checkout`. `AUTO_MERGE` is written by the `ort` merge machinery when it leaves conflicts, and on Git 2.55 also by a clean `git stash pop`. It holds a tree.

beats.text: The property that matters in an incident: these names, HEAD excepted, aren't starting points for reachability. An object is reachable when a starting point leads to it, and garbage collection deletes what nothing reaches. The starting points are refs/, HEAD, the reflogs and the index. So FETCH_HEAD, ORIG_HEAD and AUTO_MERGE protect nothing from garbage collection beyond the grace period.
beats.tele: The property that matters in an incident: these names, HEAD excepted, aren't starting points for reachability. An object is reachable when a starting point leads to it, and garbage collection deletes what nothing reaches. The starting points are `refs/`, HEAD, the reflogs and the index. So `FETCH_HEAD`, `ORIG_HEAD` and `AUTO_MERGE` protect nothing from garbage collection beyond the grace period.

beats.text: Third topic: reflogs. In one sentence: a reflog is an append-only record of the values a ref has had, one file per ref under logs/ in the files format, written whenever the ref moves. core.logAllRefUpdates is true in a repository with a working tree, which creates logs for HEAD, branches, remote-tracking branches and notes.
beats.tele: Third topic: reflogs. In one sentence: a reflog is an append-only record of the values a ref has had, one file per ref under `logs/` in the `files` format, written whenever the ref moves. `core.logAllRefUpdates` is `true` in a repository with a working tree, which creates logs for HEAD, branches, remote-tracking branches and notes.

beats.text: The value always extends this to every ref under refs/. A bare repository, one without a working tree, has it off and keeps no reflogs by default. Tags get no reflog under the default setting, and deleting a branch deletes its log.
beats.tele: The value `always` extends this to every ref under `refs/`. A bare repository, one without a working tree, has it off and keeps no reflogs by default. Tags get no reflog under the default setting, and deleting a branch deletes its log.

beats.text: When should you not use the plumbing? git update-ref on the checked-out branch and git symbolic-ref HEAD move the branch and leave the index and the working tree behind. Treat them as repairs. Use git switch and git reset for daily work.
beats.tele: When should you not use the plumbing? `git update-ref` on the checked-out branch and `git symbolic-ref HEAD` move the branch and leave the index and the working tree behind. Treat them as repairs. Use `git switch` and `git reset` for daily work.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy is signposts. Each carries a name and points at one house, an object. A few point at another signpost: those are symbolic refs. Moving a signpost is cheap and changes no house.

beats.text: The analogy breaks at demolition. In Git, a house that no signpost leads to is eventually torn down. That was the previous video.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. Picture a platform team that lists stale branches for a weekly clean-up report. Their first script walked .git/refs/heads and missed most branches on the build server, where refs are packed. The replacement is one command: git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate --format='%(committerdate:short) %(refname:short)' refs/heads, which lists branches by age and needs no parsing. git branch --format and git tag --format accept the same language.

beats.text: Let's land this. A ref is a name, where it's kept is Git's business, and you ask Git.
beats.tele: Let's land this. A ref is a name, where it's kept is Git's business, and you ask Git.

beats.text: You should now be able to say:
beats.tele: You should now be able to say:

beats.text: A ref is a loose file, a line in packed-refs, or both; the loose file is read first.
beats.tele: A ref is a loose file, a line in `packed-refs`, or both; the loose file is read first.

beats.text: Plumbing reads and writes refs in every format: for-each-ref, show-ref, update-ref, symbolic-ref.
beats.tele: Plumbing reads and writes refs in every format: `for-each-ref`, `show-ref`, `update-ref`, `symbolic-ref`.

beats.text: Since Git 2.46, only FETCH_HEAD and MERGE_HEAD are pseudorefs; ORIG_HEAD and its relatives are root refs.
beats.tele: Since Git 2.46, only `FETCH_HEAD` and `MERGE_HEAD` are pseudorefs; `ORIG_HEAD` and its relatives are root refs.

beats.text: Apart from HEAD, none of them keeps an object alive.
beats.tele: Apart from HEAD, none of them keeps an object alive.

beats.text: Reflogs are files under logs/; tags have none by default, and a deleted branch loses its own.
beats.tele: Reflogs are files under `logs/`; tags have none by default, and a deleted branch loses its own.
